standard.title: Culture shapes scientific knowledge
standard.description: investigate how cultural perspectives and world views influence the development of scientific knowledge
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can examine why scientific advances depend on collaboration and building on prior work (AC9S5H01). They have not yet investigated how cultural perspectives and world views specifically shape which questions are asked and how knowledge develops.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate how cultural perspectives and world views influence the development of scientific knowledge.

nodes.label: Scientists bring perspectives to their work
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that scientists' personal beliefs, cultural backgrounds and societal contexts influence the questions they pursue
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example where a scientist's personal beliefs or cultural background influenced the questions they chose to investigate
nodes.typical_width: Compare two scientists whose different perspectives led them to pursue different questions or approaches; explain how perspective shaped each
wider: Explore how Richard Levins' political views led him to focus on population ecology, or how Joseph Rotblat refused to work on atomic bomb science
Investigate how David Unaipon used cultural knowledge of boomerang aerodynamics to conceptualise early flight technology
Research how a scientist's disciplinary training shapes the questions they see as worth investigating

response_modes.reason: Students need to accumulate a range of scientist examples — across gender, culture, discipline, era — to see that perspective-shaping of scientific questions is a general phenomenon, not a biographical curiosity. Two examples (Levins, Rotblat; Unaipon) give different dimensions: political values, cultural knowledge, disciplinary lens. Each adds a distinct facet to the repertoire.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The David Unaipon direction is particularly rich — it connects cultural knowledge (boomerang aerodynamics) to technological innovation (flight), giving advancing students a concrete case where Indigenous knowledge directly shaped a scientific question. This is deeper than a biographical example and connects to AC9S7H01's perspective thread.
success_criteria: Names a specific example where perspective influenced a scientific question or approach
Explains the connection between the perspective and the scientific work
Does not treat perspective as automatically introducing bias or error

nodes.label: Cultural knowledge systems contribute to science
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how knowledge systems from different cultures contribute to scientific understanding
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one example where cultural knowledge has contributed to scientific understanding; explain the contribution
nodes.typical_width: Investigate First Nations Australians' classification systems and explain how they differ in context and purpose from Linnaean taxonomy; identify what each contributes
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians have developed sustainable harvesting practices and cultural protocols based on deep ecological understandings
Explore the work of Wang Zhenyi, including her experiments on lunar eclipses, as an example of non-Western scientific contribution
Compare how different cultural knowledge systems approach the same natural phenomenon and what each reveals

response_modes.reason: Students commonly hold a deficit view — that cultural knowledge is either 'real science' or 'not science' — rather than understanding that different knowledge systems ask different questions and contribute different insights. Investigating multiple cultural contexts (First Nations classification, Wang Zhenyi, sustainable harvesting) helps students see that contributions are genuine and varied, not tokenistic. Single-context teaching reinforces the deficit view; breadth resolves it.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Wang Zhenyi is a genuinely rich direction — an 18th-century Chinese female scholar conducting systematic experiments on lunar eclipses, representing a non-Western scientific tradition that is largely invisible in Australian curricula. Advancing students who investigate her work gain both a concrete example of cultural contribution and a prompt to question whose knowledge counts as science.
success_criteria: Names a specific cultural knowledge contribution to scientific understanding
Explains what the contribution is rather than just naming the culture
Does not frame cultural knowledge as inferior to or separate from science

nodes.label: Different perspectives on science-society issues
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why different people hold different perspectives on science-related issues and why recognising this matters
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one science-society issue where different groups hold different perspectives; explain why the perspectives differ
nodes.typical_width: Analyse a science-society issue (e.g. biological controls for invasive species) from at least two stakeholder perspectives; explain why each perspective exists and why recognising multiple perspectives matters
wider: Consider why it is important to recognise different perspectives on the introduction of biological controls to eradicate an invasive species
Investigate a local science-society issue and map the different stakeholder perspectives, explaining the values behind each
Evaluate whether a scientific decision-making process adequately considered diverse perspectives and explain what was missing

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe different perspectives without explaining why the perspectives differ — they list viewpoints rather than reasoning through the values, knowledge systems, and stakes that produce them. Scaffolding the reasoning (what does this group know, what do they value, what are they protecting?) moves students from perspective inventory to perspective analysis.

success_criteria: Identifies a science-society issue with multiple perspectives
Explains why different groups hold different views
Recognises that considering multiple perspectives improves decision-making

nodes.label: Culture shapes the development of scientific knowledge
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how cultural perspectives and world views have influenced the development of scientific knowledge across multiple examples
nodes.minimum_width: Explain how cultural perspectives influenced the development of scientific knowledge in one specific case, connecting the perspective to the knowledge outcome
nodes.typical_width: Compare two cases where cultural perspectives shaped scientific knowledge differently; explain the mechanism of influence in each
wider: Investigate how First Nations ecological knowledge has shaped contemporary conservation science in a specific region
Research how cultural context shaped scientific priorities in a historical case (e.g. space race, colonial-era natural history) and evaluate the consequences
Construct an argument about why diversity of perspectives strengthens scientific knowledge overall

response_modes.reason: This node integrates the personal perspective thread (Node 1), the cultural knowledge systems thread (Node 2), and the science-society thread (Node 3) into a coherent explanation of how culture shapes scientific knowledge development. Students who can address each thread separately but cannot synthesise them into a general explanatory account have not met the descriptor's investigative demand.

The argument-construction direction — why diversity of perspectives strengthens scientific knowledge — requires explicit scaffolding of the claim-evidence-reasoning structure. Students need support connecting the empirical examples from earlier nodes to the general claim, not just listing them.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The colonial-era natural history direction is rich for advancing students — it surfaces how cultural priorities (European expansion, taxonomic imperialism) shaped which knowledge was collected, preserved and valued. This connects to AC9S7H01 and gives students a critical lens on the history of science that goes well beyond the minimum explanation task.
success_criteria: Explains how a cultural perspective influenced the development of specific scientific knowledge
Connects the perspective to the knowledge outcome rather than just describing each separately
